headline: High-risk pair: shared orchestration and MCP-enabled tool paths create default data-leakage, prompt-injection, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can wire developer-defined tools as nodes and has no self-isolation; LightAgent exposes MCP over stdio/SSE and runtime hooks can observe/replace/block lifecycle payloads. That creates a plausible default bridge where LightAgent content can reach LangGraph nodes and be treated as instructions. The interaction is inferred, not directly sandboxed.
conditions: IF LightAgent payloads are forwarded into LangGraph nodes without provenance tagging, injection risk is active.
IF LangGraph nodes parse file or tool output as trusted instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer execution.
mitigations: Add provenance tags to every cross-agent message.
Insert a 1-line allowlist filter for tool directives.
Disable automatic execution of model-generated commands.
Review one representative message path for instruction/data separation.
requires-engineering: add signed message envelopes between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph reads and writes application-defined files, handles model provider API keys, and uses broad network egress; LightAgent touches conversations, long-term memory, trace data, tool calls/results, and provenance metadata, with MCP and streaming APIs. If they share a workspace or state store, sensitive data can flow from one agent into the other and out over networked inference paths.
conditions: IF both agents share the same workspace or checkpointer-backed state, leakage becomes active.
IF LightAgent forwards trace data or memory into LangGraph-managed tools, sensitive context can be exposed.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and state stores.
Rotate any exposed API keys.
Disable sharing of trace data across agents.
Audit one end-to-end data path for secrets.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent encryption and access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and subprocess execution, and both support multiple instances. LangGraph can write application-defined files; LightAgent can use MCP and runtime hooks that can replace lifecycle payloads. Without explicit locking or isolation, concurrent writes or tool-side effects can collide on shared mutable resources.
conditions: IF both agents target the same filesystem or mutable workflow state, write conflicts are possible.
IF either agent mutates shared tool state without locks, race conditions can corrupt outputs.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Run only one writer per shared resource.
Check for duplicate subprocess side effects.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework for stateful long-running agents, so its outputs can become downstream inputs by design; LightAgent is a tool-calling agent with MCP and runtime hooks that can act on lifecycle payloads. If LightAgent treats LangGraph output as authoritative, an upstream mistake can cascade into incorrect tool actions or workflow corruption.
conditions: IF LightAgent consumes LangGraph output without verification, errors can propagate downstream.
IF LangGraph emits unvalidated facts or plans into LightAgent tool calls, the pair can execute incorrect actions.
mitigations: Require a verification step before any tool action.
Add a human review gate for high-impact outputs.
Log and diff upstream claims against source data.
Limit automatic execution to read-only tools.
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware validation.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles touch sensitive operational data, but only LightAgent explicitly lists conversations, long-term memory, trace data, and tool results; LangGraph handles application-defined graph state and model-provider secrets. The profiles do not document residency or retention alignment, so a mismatch is plausible but not proven. Uncertainty escalates above low because the data classes are broad and persistent.
conditions: IF either agent stores EU PII or regulated data in a region or service not approved for that class, compliance risk is active.
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the shared workflow state, subject-rights handling can fail.
mitigations: Inventory data classes for one workflow.
Check retention settings in both runtimes.
Disable logging of sensitive fields.
Confirm residency for any regulated dataset.
requires-engineering: align DPA, residency, and retention controls.
